description.context: When you write df.write.partitionBy('region').parquet('path/'), Spark does not just write one parquet file. It creates a DIRECTORY for each unique value of the partition column, and writes the matching rows into that directory's parquet files. The directory name encodes the partition column and value as 'region=NORTH' (the format is column=value). This means later queries can SKIP entire directories without reading them — that is the foundation of partition pruning. The partition columns are NOT stored inside the parquet files; they live only in the directory names.

fields.label: What does this directory structure tell you?
options: The 'region=NORTH' folder names are just labels for human readability; the actual partitioning lives inside the parquet files. Spark needs to read every part-*.parquet file regardless of which region you query.

Each region's rows live in their own directory. region is a partition column — its values appear in directory names but not inside the parquet files. Queries filtering by region skip the other directories entirely.
The directory tree shows a corrupted write — there should be one parquet file at the top level with all data. The region= folders indicate that partitionBy() failed and wrote duplicates.
region= directories store metadata only; the actual data is in the _SUCCESS file at the top level. Queries read _SUCCESS and follow pointers into the region directories.
fields.correctAnswer: Each region's rows live in their own directory. region is a partition column — its values appear in directory names but not inside the parquet files. Queries filtering by region skip the other directories entirely.
fields.rationale: partitionBy('region') tells Spark to physically split rows by region value. Each unique region gets its own directory, named 'region=VALUE'. NORTH rows are written to region=NORTH/ as parquet files; SOUTH rows go to region=SOUTH/. The region column is NOT stored inside the parquet files (Spark reconstructs the value from the directory name when reading). When a later query filters .filter(col('region') == 'NORTH'), Spark reads ONLY the region=NORTH/ directory and skips the others — this is partition pruning. The _SUCCESS file is just an empty marker confirming the write completed.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats directories as cosmetic. The directory structure IS the partitioning.

Option C: Treats normal output as corruption. region= dirs are the expected partitionBy result.

Option D: Invents a metadata-pointer system. _SUCCESS is just a write-complete marker.

description.context: A column can be a PARTITION COLUMN (values appear in directory names) or a DATA COLUMN (values stored inside parquet files). When you write df.write.partitionBy('region').parquet(...), region becomes a partition column — it is removed from the parquet file's columns and lives only in the directory name. When you write df.write.parquet(...) without partitionBy, every column is a data column — all values live inside the parquet files. The two have very different read costs: a filter on a partition column can prune entire directories; a filter on a data column must read parquet files (though file-level statistics may still help skip some).
description.task: What is the structural difference between Layout A and Layout B?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code A: meters.write.partitionBy('region').parquet('layout_a/')

Code B: meters.write.parquet('layout_b/')

Schema: meter_id, daily_kw, region, customer_type

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Same dataset written two ways — once with partitionBy('region'), once without — visible at the directory level

fields.label: What is the structural difference between Layout A and Layout B?
options: Layout A has region as partition column (values in directory names, not in parquet schema). Layout B has region as data column (values inside parquet files). Filters on region prune directories in A but read files in B.

Layout A has FEWER columns than Layout B because partitionBy() drops the region column entirely; queries against Layout A cannot return region values when read back. Layout B keeps all columns and is generally preferred.
Layout A is broken — region should be present in BOTH directory names AND parquet files for proper partitioning. Layout B is the correctly-written version that includes the column everywhere.
Both layouts behave identically because Spark transparently abstracts directory structure from the user. The difference is purely cosmetic and does not affect query performance.
fields.correctAnswer: Layout A has region as partition column (values in directory names, not in parquet schema). Layout B has region as data column (values inside parquet files). Filters on region prune directories in A but read files in B.
fields.rationale: In Layout A, region is a partition column: its values appear in directory names (region=NORTH/) but are removed from the parquet file's schema. When Spark reads, it reconstructs region from the directory name. Queries filtering on region can skip whole directories — partition pruning. In Layout B, region is a data column stored inside every parquet file alongside the others. Queries filtering on region must read parquet files (though file-level min/max stats may skip some). The trade-off: A is faster for region-filtered queries; B keeps all data co-located if your queries don't filter by region.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Treats partitionBy as data loss. Spark reconstructs the partition column on read; no information is lost.

Option C: Treats partition columns as needing duplication. The whole point is they live in directories ONLY.

Option D: Treats the layouts as identical. Read performance differs significantly for filtered queries.

description.context: When you query a partitioned table with a filter on the partition column, the Spark plan shows whether pruning happened. Look at the FileScan line for a field called 'PartitionFilters: [...]'. If your filter is in this list, Spark only read the matching partition directories — pruning worked. PartitionFilters is different from 'PushedFilters' or 'dataFilters' (those refer to file-level filtering on data columns). The most reliable proof of partition pruning is the metric 'PartitionCount: N' showing how many directories were actually accessed.
description.task: What does this plan tell you about whether partition pruning worked?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code: spark.read.parquet('s3://nordgrid/bronze/meters/').filter(col('region') == 'NORTH').count()

Total Partitions: 4 (NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST)

Partition Layout: region=*/part-*.parquet

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Plan from a NordGrid query filtering on the partition column region; partition pruning visible in PartitionFilters and PartitionCount

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
== Physical Plan ==
AdaptiveSparkPlan isFinalPlan=true
+- HashAggregate(keys=[], functions=[count(1)])
   +- Exchange SinglePartition
      +- HashAggregate(keys=[], functions=[partial_count(1)])
         +- ColumnarToRow
            +- FileScan parquet [meter_id#0, daily_kw#3]
               PartitionFilters: [isnotnull(region#5), (region#5 = NORTH)]
               PushedFilters: []
               PartitionCount: 1
               Location: InMemoryFileIndex[s3://nordgrid/bronze/meters/]

fields.label: What does this plan tell you about whether partition pruning worked?
options: Pruning did not work; PartitionFilters being non-empty means Spark TRIED to prune but failed. Look at PushedFilters being empty as confirmation; queries with no PushedFilters always read all partitions.

Pruning is unconfirmable from this plan; PartitionFilters is informational only. The only reliable evidence is the actual file-listing operation in the Spark UI's storage tab, which is not visible here.

Pruning worked. PartitionFilters: [region = NORTH] shows the predicate is pushed to the partition layer. PartitionCount: 1 confirms only ONE partition directory was read out of 4 total. Spark skipped the SOUTH/EAST/WEST directories entirely.

Partial pruning worked at the directory level but Spark still read every parquet file inside region=NORTH/. The PartitionCount: 1 refers to logical partitions only; the physical file count was unchanged.
fields.correctAnswer: Pruning worked. PartitionFilters: [region = NORTH] shows the predicate is pushed to the partition layer. PartitionCount: 1 confirms only ONE partition directory was read out of 4 total. Spark skipped the SOUTH/EAST/WEST directories entirely.
fields.rationale: Two pieces of evidence confirm pruning. First, PartitionFilters: [region = NORTH] shows the filter on the partition column was applied at the partition-discovery layer (not at the row-filtering layer). Second, PartitionCount: 1 shows Spark touched exactly ONE partition directory of the 4 in the table. SOUTH, EAST, WEST were skipped entirely — Spark didn't even list their files. The empty PushedFilters is normal: there's no data-column filter to push, only the partition filter. Reading PartitionFilters is the standard way to verify pruning; reading PartitionCount is the standard way to confirm how many directories were touched.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Reverses the meaning of PartitionFilters; non-empty means pruning happened, not failed.

Option B: Treats PartitionFilters as cosmetic; it is the authoritative pruning indicator.

Option D: Conflates partition count with file count; PartitionCount 1 means 1 directory was read.

tasks.title: The Filter That Did Not Prune

description.context: Partition pruning ONLY works when the filter is on a partition column. If you filter on a data column (a column stored inside parquet files, not in directory names), Spark must read the parquet files to apply the filter. The plan signal is clear: a partition-column filter appears in PartitionFilters and shows PartitionCount < total. A data-column filter appears in PushedFilters or as a separate Filter operator, and PartitionCount equals the total number of partitions because Spark visited every directory.
description.task: Why does Plan B read all 4 partitions despite having a filter, and what is the lesson?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Table Layout: partitioned by region (4 directories: NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST)

Code A: df.filter(col('region') == 'NORTH').count()

Code B: df.filter(col('customer_type') == 'RESIDENTIAL').count()

Schema: meter_id, daily_kw, region (partition col), customer_type (data col)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Two plans for similar queries — one filters on partition column (prunes), one filters on data column (does not prune)

fields.label: Why does Plan B read all 4 partitions despite having a filter, and what is the lesson?
options: Plan B's PartitionCount: 4 is misleading — Spark still pruned at the file level (PushedFilters is non-empty). The lesson: PushedFilters and PartitionFilters are equivalent forms of pruning and either one is sufficient.

Plan B's filter is too complex; equality filters never prune partitions. Only range filters (>, <, BETWEEN) trigger pruning. The lesson: rewrite as customer_type BETWEEN 'A' AND 'Z' to enable pruning.

Plan B fails to prune because the filter has no IsNotNull added by Catalyst. Without IsNotNull, partition pruning logic refuses to fire. The lesson: always add explicit isNotNull() before equality filters.

Plan B's filter is on customer_type, a data column stored inside parquet files. Spark cannot prune directories based on data columns — it must visit all 4 partitions and read parquet files. The lesson: only partition-column filters prune directories.
fields.correctAnswer: Plan B's filter is on customer_type, a data column stored inside parquet files. Spark cannot prune directories based on data columns — it must visit all 4 partitions and read parquet files. The lesson: only partition-column filters prune directories.
fields.rationale: Plan A's filter (region == 'NORTH') is on the partition column, so Spark applies it at directory-discovery time and skips 3 of 4 directories. PartitionCount: 1 confirms. Plan B's filter (customer_type == 'RESIDENTIAL') is on a data column. Spark cannot know which partitions contain RESIDENTIAL rows without reading the files; the customer_type filter goes into PushedFilters where the parquet reader applies it after reading the files. PartitionCount: 4 confirms every directory was visited. Only filters on partition columns can prune directories — filters on data columns can at best skip rows within files via PushedFilters.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats PushedFilters and PartitionFilters as equivalent; they operate at different layers.

Option B: Invents an equality-vs-range pruning rule that doesn't exist.

Option C: Treats IsNotNull as the trigger; Catalyst adds it automatically anyway.

description.context: Partitioning has a sweet spot. Too coarse (one giant partition) means no pruning. Too granular (thousands of tiny partitions) creates the SMALL-FILE PROBLEM. Spark must list every partition directory before reading, and each parquet file has ~1KB of metadata overhead per file. With 8760 hourly partitions × 4MB per partition, you get 8760 file-listing operations and 35MB of metadata overhead just to read 35GB of data. The general guideline is that each partition should hold 100MB-1GB of data; below that, partition overhead dominates the read.
description.task: Why is the hourly layout 8× slower than daily partitioning, and what is the lesson?

Total Partitions: 8760 (24 hours × 365 days)

Total Data Size: 35 GB

Average Partition Size: 4 MB

Average File Size: 4 MB (one file per partition)

Observed Full Table Scan Time: 12 minutes (vs 90 seconds for daily partitioning)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Layout with 8760 hourly partitions for a year of NordGrid bronze data, average 4MB per partition

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
$ ls layout/year=2025/month=04/day=30/
  hour=00/part-00000.parquet  (4.1 MB)
  hour=01/part-00000.parquet  (3.8 MB)
  hour=02/part-00000.parquet  (4.2 MB)
  ...
  hour=23/part-00000.parquet  (3.9 MB)

# Total layout shape:
#   8760 partitions (24 hours × 365 days)
#   8760 parquet files (one per partition)

#   Daily partitioning:     90 seconds (for the same 35 GB)

fields.label: Why is the hourly layout 8× slower than daily partitioning, and what is the lesson?
options: Hourly partitioning produces 8760 tiny files. Spark must list 8760 directories and read 8760 file footers before any actual data reading. Per-file overhead dominates total runtime when files are small. Partitions need ≥100MB.
Hourly partitioning is fundamentally faster than daily; the slow timing is environmental. Re-run the test with a warm filesystem cache and the hourly layout will outperform daily by 8×.

Hourly partitioning produces correctly-sized partitions; the issue is that S3 charges per LIST operation across all directories. The 8× slowdown is monetary cost reflected in latency. Switching to local HDFS would eliminate the difference.
The slow timing comes from too FEW partitions, not too many; 8760 partitions is below Spark's default parallelism of 200K. Increase spark.default.parallelism to compensate for the under-parallelism.
fields.correctAnswer: Hourly partitioning produces 8760 tiny files. Spark must list 8760 directories and read 8760 file footers before any actual data reading. Per-file overhead dominates total runtime when files are small. Partitions need ≥100MB.
fields.rationale: The small-file problem has three components. (1) File listing: Spark must enumerate 8760 directories before reading anything; this scales linearly. (2) Metadata read: each parquet file has a ~1KB footer Spark must parse to know its schema and stats; 8760 files = 8.6MB of metadata reads scattered across the cluster. (3) Task scheduling: each file becomes (at minimum) one task; scheduling 8760 tiny tasks costs more than scheduling 365 medium tasks. Daily partitioning would produce 365 partitions of ~96MB each — close to the 128MB target — and all three overheads drop. The general guideline: target 100MB-1GB per partition.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Treats slowness as cache-related. Per-file overhead is structural, not environmental.

Option C: Blames S3 LIST cost; the per-file metadata read dominates regardless of filesystem.

Option D: Reverses the problem — too FEW partitions would mean too few tasks, not too many.

description.context: The opposite extreme of the small-file problem is the SINGLE-PARTITION (or unpartitioned) layout. When a table has no partition columns or has one giant partition, queries cannot prune anything — every read must scan the full dataset. The small-file problem trades off against the no-pruning problem: too many partitions wastes overhead, but too few prevents Spark from skipping data your query doesn't need. The right partition strategy puts data into 100MB-1GB chunks aligned with how queries filter. A 35GB table with no partition columns will full-scan for EVERY query that needs ANY subset of the data.
description.task: What is the problem with this layout, and how does it differ from SLJ3.1's small-file problem?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code: meters.write.parquet('layout/')

Total Partitions: 1 (no partitioning)

Total Data Size: 35 GB

File Count: 200 files of ~175MB each (one per shuffle output partition)

Common Query Pattern: .filter(col('region') == 'NORTH').count()

Observed Query Time: 8 minutes (full 35GB scan every time)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Layout with 1 unpartitioned 35GB parquet write; queries always full-scan

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
$ ls layout/
  part-00000.parquet  (174 MB)
  part-00001.parquet  (176 MB)
  ...
  part-00199.parquet  (175 MB)
  _SUCCESS

# Layout shape:
#   No partition columns (no region=*/ or date=*/ subdirectories)
#   200 parquet files at the top level
#   Total: 35 GB
#
# Query plan for: filter(region == 'NORTH').count()
+- FileScan parquet [meter_id, daily_kw, region, customer_type]
   PartitionFilters: []          ← empty (no partition columns)
   PushedFilters: [EqualTo(region, NORTH)]
   PartitionCount: 1             ← whole table is 'one partition'
   Bytes read: 35 GB             ← full scan every time

fields.label: What is the problem with this layout, and how does it differ from SLJ3.1's small-file problem?
options: 200 files × 175 MB each is the optimal layout; no partitioning needed for this dataset shape. The 8-minute query time is unavoidable for 35GB of data and reflects normal Spark behavior. No change needed.
200 files × 175 MB each is the optimal layout; no partitioning needed. The 8-minute query time is unavoidable for 35GB of data and reflects normal Spark behavior. No change needed.
The layout is correct but the query is wrong; rewrite as filter('region == NORTH', filter_pushdown=True) to enable pruning. The standard filter() does not push down without the explicit flag.

No partition columns means no pruning is possible; every query scans 35GB. PartitionCount=1 confirms the whole table is one logical partition. SLJ3.1 had too many tiny partitions; this has too few. Both wrong, opposite reasons.
fields.correctAnswer: No partition columns means no pruning is possible; every query scans 35GB. PartitionCount=1 confirms the whole table is one logical partition. SLJ3.1 had too many tiny partitions; this has too few. Both wrong, opposite reasons.
fields.rationale: The two failure modes are opposites. SLJ3.1's hourly layout had 8760 tiny partitions: pruning could work but per-file overhead dominated. This layout has 0 partition columns: file sizes are correct (175MB, near target) but no directory pruning is possible. Every query reads all 35GB even when only a small slice is needed. The fix: add partitionBy('region') or partitionBy('date') so the filter can prune at directory-discovery time. Note that PushedFilters does help — the parquet reader skips rows within files that fail the predicate — but it still has to OPEN every file and read column statistics. Partition pruning skips even the file-open.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats PushedFilters as eliminating reads. Pushdown skips rows but still opens files.

Option B: Treats the layout as optimal. File size is fine; missing partition columns is the issue.

Option C: Invents a filter_pushdown flag. Pushdown happens automatically on built-in expressions.

description.context: Partition-column selection has rules. The cardinality (number of distinct values) of the partition column directly becomes the number of directories on disk. A column like meter_id has 500K distinct values — partitioning by it creates 500K directories, each holding one or two rows. This is the small-file problem multiplied by 1000. The general rule: partition columns should have BETWEEN ~10 and ~10,000 distinct values for production datasets. Below that, you don't get enough pruning; above that, you trigger the small-file disaster.
description.task: What is wrong, and what is the rule?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code: meters.write.partitionBy('meter_id').parquet('layout/')

Distinct Meter Ids: 500000

Directories Created: 500000

Average Rows Per Partition: 1 (one row per meter)

Average File Size Per Partition: 300 bytes

Write Time: 47 minutes for 500K-row dataset (vs 8 seconds with date partitioning)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Layout where meter_id (500K distinct values) was used as partition column, creating 500K directories

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
$ ls layout/ | head -5
  meter_id=ABC0000001/
  meter_id=ABC0000002/
  meter_id=ABC0000003/
  meter_id=ABC0000004/
  meter_id=ABC0000005/
  ... (500,000 directories total)

$ ls layout/meter_id=ABC0000001/
  part-00000.parquet  (304 bytes)

# Query: filter(col('region') == 'NORTH').count()
+- FileScan parquet [meter_id, daily_kw, region, customer_type]
   PartitionFilters: []                  ← region not partitioned
   PushedFilters: [EqualTo(region, NORTH)]
   PartitionCount: 500000                ← reads ALL 500K directories
   Files read: 500000 (304 bytes each)
   Total bytes read: 152 MB
   Total query time: 22 minutes

fields.label: What is wrong, and what is the rule?
options: Partitioning works correctly; the slow query time is expected for 500K-row datasets. Rule: keep dataset sizes below 100K rows OR partition by a high-cardinality column to spread work.

meter_id has 500K distinct values; using it as partition column creates 500K directories with one row each. Per-directory overhead × 500K destroys performance. Rule: 10-10,000 distinct values, not 500K.
The 500K directories are correct; the query is the bug. Rewrite as filter(col('meter_id').isin([...])) to enable pruning across the meter_id partition column for region-filtered queries.
meter_id is a string column; partitioning by string columns is forbidden because Spark cannot type the directory names properly. Rule: only partition by numeric or date columns.
fields.correctAnswer: meter_id has 500K distinct values; using it as partition column creates 500K directories with one row each. Per-directory overhead × 500K destroys performance. Rule: 10-10,000 distinct values, not 500K.
fields.rationale: Cardinality is the load-bearing rule. partitionBy(col) creates one directory per unique value. meter_id has 500K unique values, so 500K directories are created. Each directory holds ~1 row in a tiny file. Read cost: list 500K directories, open 500K files, schedule 500K tasks. Writes are equally bad — 47 minutes for what should be 8 seconds. The query above STILL needs to scan all 500K directories because it filters on region (a different column), and the filter doesn't help with the per-directory overhead. The rule: partition columns should produce 10-10,000 directories. Date (daily) gives ~365 per year. Region gives 4. customer_type gives 4. meter_id gives 500K — wrong by 50× minimum.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats large datasets as needing more partitions; the relationship inverts at high cardinality.

Option C: Treats the layout as correct; the cardinality is the failure.

Option D: Invents a no-strings-as-partition rule that doesn't exist.

description.context: After learning what NOT to do (high cardinality, single column, hourly), the canonical good pattern emerges: date + region. partitionBy('date', 'region') uses TWO partition columns. Spark creates a nested directory structure: date=*/region=*/. The combined cardinality is manageable (365 days × 4 regions = 1460 directories per year), and the two columns match how queries actually filter — most NordGrid queries are 'a time range AND a region'. Either filter alone prunes substantially; both together prune almost everything except the slice the query needs.
description.task: Why does this pattern work well for NordGrid's typical queries?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Code: meters.write.partitionBy('date', 'region').parquet('layout/')

Date Range: 2025-01-01 to 2025-12-31 (365 days)

Regions: [NORTH, SOUTH, EAST, WEST]

Total Partitions: 1460 (365 × 4)

Average Partition Size: 180MB

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Layout with partitionBy('date', 'region') showing the canonical two-column pattern at NordGrid scale

evidence.label: Snippet
evidence.content:
$ ls -R layout/
layout/date=2025-04-30/region=NORTH/
  part-00000.parquet  (~180 MB)
layout/date=2025-04-30/region=SOUTH/
  part-00000.parquet  (~180 MB)
... (similar for EAST, WEST)

# Query A: filter(col('date') == '2025-04-30').count()
   PartitionFilters: [(date = 2025-04-30)]
   PartitionCount: 4         ← read 4 directories (all regions for that date)

# Query B: filter((date == '2025-04-30') & (region == 'NORTH')).count()
   PartitionFilters: [(date = 2025-04-30), (region = NORTH)]
   PartitionCount: 1         ← read 1 directory only

# Query C: filter(col('region') == 'NORTH').count()
   PartitionFilters: [(region = NORTH)]
   PartitionCount: 365       ← read 365 directories (all dates for NORTH)

fields.label: Why does this pattern work well for NordGrid's typical queries?
options: The two-column nested layout supports three access patterns. Time-range queries get 4 partitions. Point queries get 1 partition. Full-region scans get 365 partitions. Either filter alone prunes substantially.

Two-column partitioning is purely cosmetic — internally Spark treats it identically to no partitioning. The PartitionCount values shown are misleading; actual scan times are similar across all three queries shown above.

This pattern works because date is FIRST in partitionBy(); reversing the order to partitionBy('region', 'date') would prevent pruning entirely. The first partition column has special pruning privileges.
1460 partitions is too many; this layout suffers from the small-file problem covered in SLJ3.1. Switch to date-only partitioning (365 directories) to fix the per-directory overhead issue.
fields.correctAnswer: The two-column nested layout supports three access patterns. Time-range queries get 4 partitions. Point queries get 1 partition. Full-region scans get 365 partitions. Either filter alone prunes substantially.
fields.rationale: The date+region pattern aligns with NordGrid's actual query mix. Time-range queries (daily reports) prune on date. Region-specific queries (operational dashboards) prune on region. Combined queries (regulatory reports for region X on date Y) prune on both. The 1460 total partitions × 180MB each gives partition sizes near the 100MB-1GB sweet spot. Pruning works equally well filtering on either column alone or both together. If the query mix were different — say 95% by customer_type with date irrelevant — the right partition scheme would be different. Layout follows queries.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Treats partitioning as cosmetic; PartitionCount drives actual read scope.

Option C: Invents an order-of-columns rule. Both orderings prune similarly; nested order affects directory layout, not pruning capability.

Option D: Treats 1460 partitions as too many; 180MB/partition is near optimal.

description.context: Time to put it all together. The senior engineer hands the junior a pointer to NordGrid's actual bronze meter layer. The junior must read the layout — directory structure, partition counts, file sizes — and answer four questions about whether it follows the rules learned in SLJ1-SLJ4. Some things are right; some are wrong; the junior must read carefully.

description.context: The senior engineer shows the junior two different layouts of the same NordGrid 500K-meter dataset. Layout A partitions by date only (365 directories). Layout B partitions by date AND region (1460 directories). Same source data, same total bytes (~268GB). The senior asks: which layout favors which query patterns, what is the file-count trade-off, and which is the right pick for NordGrid given how queries actually filter? This is the synthesis exercise — every concept from SLJ1-SLJ4 applies.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Same 268GB NordGrid dataset written two ways — date-only partitioning vs date+region partitioning

evidence.content:
# Layout A — date only
#   meters.write.partitionBy('date').parquet('layout_a/')

$ ls layout_a/date=2025-04-30/
  part-00000.parquet  (185 MB)
  part-00001.parquet  (180 MB)
  part-00002.parquet  (175 MB)
  part-00003.parquet  (190 MB)
  Average partition size: ~730 MB across 4 files

# Total: 365 partitions, 1460 files (~4 per partition)

# Layout B — date and region
#   meters.write.partitionBy('date', 'region').parquet('layout_b/')

$ ls layout_b/date=2025-04-30/region=NORTH/
  part-00000.parquet  (180 MB)
  Average partition size: ~180 MB (one region's data)

# Total: 1,460 partitions, 1,460 files (1 per partition)

# NordGrid query mix (from production logs):
#   60% queries: filter on date range only (e.g., 'last 7 days')
#   30% queries: filter on date AND region (regional reports)
#   10% queries: filter on region only (rare, full-history)
